snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philip
snapshots.body: Philip II of Macedon, attacked by his own guard Pausanias after being permitted to suffer an insult from Attalus and his friends.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pausanias (assassin of Philip)
snapshots.body: Attacked Philip of Macedon after being permitted to suffer an insult from Attalus and his friends -- the historical assassin of Philip II, identified here by the surrounding narrative rather than an epithet. Two different, unrelated men also named Pausanias appear elsewhere in Book 5: a Spartan king, and the regent who commanded at Plataea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Attalus
snapshots.body: Insulted Pausanias, with the friends who joined him, provoking the attack on Philip of Macedon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyntas the Little
snapshots.body: Attacked by Derdas after boasting of having enjoyed Derdas's youth. A different, unrelated Amyntas -- Archelaus's own son -- is named later in the same passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Derdas
snapshots.body: Attacked Amyntas the Little after being boasted of.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Evagoras
snapshots.body: The king of Cyprus, slain by a eunuch avenging the eunuch's wife, whom Evagoras's own son had carried off.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Crataeus
snapshots.body: Attacked and killed Archelaus, ostensibly over a broken marriage promise involving Archelaus's daughters, though Aristotle judges the real cause was Crataeus's disgust at their intimate connection.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archelaus
snapshots.body: The Macedonian king killed by Crataeus; the subject of several further conspiracies recounted in Book 5 (Hellanocrates, Decamnichus) arising from broken promises and personal insults.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sirrhas
snapshots.body: The enemy Archelaus was fighting when he married his elder daughter to the king of Elymaea for military support.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arrhibaeus
snapshots.body: Named alongside Sirrhas as an enemy Archelaus was fighting when he married his elder daughter to the king of Elymaea for military support.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyntas (son of Archelaus)
snapshots.body: Archelaus's own son, married to Archelaus's younger daughter in hope of avoiding a quarrel with the son of Cleopatra. A different, unrelated Amyntas the Little is named earlier in the same passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleopatra
snapshots.body: A Macedonian royal woman, mother of the son Archelaus hoped to keep from quarrelling with his own son Amyntas -- not the later, far better-known queen of Egypt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hellanocrates of Larissa
snapshots.body: Archelaus's lover, who conspired against him after Archelaus failed to keep his promise of restoring him to his own country.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Parrhon
snapshots.body: Killed Cotys with Heracleides of Aenos to avenge their father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heracleides of Aenos
snapshots.body: Killed Cotys with Parrhon to avenge their father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cotys
snapshots.body: The Thracian king killed by Parrhon and Heracleides of Aenos in revenge for their father, and mutilated Adamas as a child, provoking Adamas's own later revolt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adamas
snapshots.body: Revolted from Cotys in revenge for being mutilated by him as a child.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megacles
snapshots.body: Attacked and killed the Penthalidae at Mitylene with his friends, after they had gone about the city assaulting people with clubs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Penthalidae
snapshots.body: A ruling clan at Mitylene, killed by Megacles and his friends after going about assaulting people with clubs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Smerdis
snapshots.body: Beaten and torn from his wife by Penthilus, whom he later killed in revenge.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Penthilus
snapshots.body: Beat Smerdis and tore him from his wife, and was later killed by him in revenge.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Decamnichus
snapshots.body: Led the assassins in the conspiracy against Archelaus, enraged after Archelaus handed him over to Euripides to be scourged for a remark about the poet's bad breath.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artapanes
snapshots.body: Conspired against and killed Xerxes, fearing he would be blamed for hanging Darius without orders.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Xerxes
snapshots.body: The Persian king, killed by Artapanes; also cited among rulers whose empires the Persian king (an earlier, unnamed reference) crushed rebellious former subjects.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Darius
snapshots.body: Hanged, apparently on Artapanes's own initiative rather than Xerxes's orders -- probably Xerxes's own son of this name, distinct from Darius I "the Great."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dion
snapshots.body: Attacked and expelled his own relative Dionysius II out of contempt for his drunkenness, landing with only a small force on the principle that even a quick death would be an honourable risk.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysius II
snapshots.body: Dionysius I's son and successor as tyrant of Syracuse, explicitly called "the younger Dionysius," attacked out of contempt and then expelled by his own relative Dion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Astyages
snapshots.body: Cyrus's grandfather and the Median king Cyrus overthrew, his power judged worn out by an effeminate life.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Seuthes
snapshots.body: A Thracian who conspired against Amadocus, the ruler whose general he was.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amadocus
snapshots.body: The Thracian ruler against whom his own general Seuthes conspired.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mithridates
snapshots.body: Conspired against Ariobarzanes out of a mix of contempt and love of gain.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariobarzanes
snapshots.body: The ruler against whom his own subordinate Mithridates conspired.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theopompus
snapshots.body: The Spartan king who further limited royal power (chiefly by establishing the Ephoralty), reasoning that a reduced but more durable kingship was a better inheritance for his sons than a greater but less secure one.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hiero
snapshots.body: Gelo's brother and successor as tyrant of Syracuse, whose spies and informers are cited as a model of tyrannical surveillance; succeeded in turn by his own brother Thrasybulus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thrasybulus (Syracuse)
snapshots.body: Hiero's brother, who flattered Gelo's son into excess in order to rule through him, provoking the family conspiracy that ended the dynasty (5:63); he later succeeded Hiero as tyrant in his own right, only to be driven out within eleven months (5:76). A different, unrelated Thrasybulus of Miletus is Book 5's other, far more frequently cited Thrasybulus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Myron
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Sicyon whose rule gave way to that of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleisthenes of Sicyon
snapshots.body: The Orthagorid tyrant of Sicyon, respected for his military ability and said to have crowned the judge who ruled against him in the games. His rule followed Myron's (5:78) within the century-long Orthagorid tyranny (5:74). A different, unrelated Cleisthenes -- his own grandson, the Athenian democratic reformer -- appears in Books 3 and 6.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antileon
snapshots.body: His tyranny at Chalcis is cited as an example of a tyranny changing into an oligarchy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleander
snapshots.body: His tyranny at Gela is cited as an example of an oligarchy changing into a tyranny.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anaxilaus
snapshots.body: His tyranny at Rhegium is cited as an example of an oligarchy changing into a tyranny.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Orthagoras
snapshots.body: Founder of the century-long Orthagorid tyranny at Sicyon, the longest-lasting of all -- attributed to the family's moderation and general observance of the laws.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Cypselidae
snapshots.body: The tyrant dynasty of Corinth founded by Cypselus, lasting seventy-three and a half years across Cypselus, Periander, and Psammetichus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Psammetichus
snapshots.body: Son of Gordius, the third and last of the Cypselid tyrants of Corinth, reigning three years after Periander.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oxylus
snapshots.body: Credited with an early law forbidding a man to borrow against a fixed portion of his property.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archilochus
snapshots.body: The poet, cited on the pleasures of leisure that follow the toil of war.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: The physician, cited as an example of a kind of "greatness" -- excellence in one's function -- that has nothing to do with physical size.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stentor
snapshots.body: The Homeric herald proverbial for a loud voice, invoked as a comparison for what statesmen wanting only more citizens would need.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sesostris
snapshots.body: The legendary Egyptian king credited with founding the warrior-versus-husbandmen class system later found in Egypt and Crete.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Italus
snapshots.body: The legendary king of Oenotria after whom Italy is said to be named; credited with converting the Oenotrians from shepherds to husbandmen and founding their common meals.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Scylax
snapshots.body: Cited for his claim that Indian kings hold no marked superiority over their subjects.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thibron
snapshots.body: Among the writers on the Spartan constitution who praised its legislator for the power hard training won the Lacedaemonians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theodorus
snapshots.body: The tragic actor, who would not let any other actor -- however minor -- perform before him, since audiences grow fond of the first voice they hear.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Odysseus
snapshots.body: The Homeric hero, quoted on the pleasure of a banquet with music.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Musaeus
snapshots.body: The legendary poet, quoted on song as one of the pleasantest things.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Olympus
snapshots.body: A musician (or composer) whose melodies are cited as proof that music can inspire real enthusiasm and moral feeling.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pauson
snapshots.body: A painter whose work young men should not be encouraged to look at, contrasted unfavourably with Polygnotus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polygnotus
snapshots.body: A painter praised for expressing moral character in his work, contrasted favourably with Pauson.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archytas
snapshots.body: Credited with inventing the child's rattle -- a toy for the infant mind, as musical education is a toy for children of a larger growth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philoxenus
snapshots.body: A dithyrambic poet who, having tried to compose his Tales in the Dorian mode, found it impossible and fell back into the more suitable Phrygian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thrasippus
snapshots.body: Dedicated a tablet commemorating his sponsorship of a chorus for Ecphantides, cited as evidence of the flute's popularity at Athens.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ecphantides
snapshots.body: The Old Comedy poet for whom Thrasippus furnished a chorus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Athene
snapshots.body: The goddess, said in myth to have invented the flute and then thrown it away, on the reasoning (Aristotle's own gloss) that flute-playing contributes nothing to the mind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: As the speaker in Plato's Republic and Laws, the source of the community-of-women-and-property proposals that occupy most of Book 2's opening critique, and of the cyclical theory of constitutional change Aristotle rebuts at the close of Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: Author of the Republic and the Laws, whose proposed constitutions are examined at length in Book 2 and revisited in Books 4 and 7; cited by name as the author distinct from his speaker Socrates.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hesiod
snapshots.body: The early Greek poet, quoted for the line "First house and wife and an ox for the plough."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charondas
snapshots.body: The lawgiver of Catana, cited in Book 1 for a term he used for household members and, in Book 2, for the laws he gave his own and other Chalcidian cities in Italy and Sicily.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epimenides the Cretan
snapshots.body: Cited for a term he used for household members, alongside Charondas.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: The poet, quoted repeatedly (Books 1, 3, 4) -- on the Cyclopes' households, on the "tribeless, lawless, hearthless" man outside the state, and on Agamemnon's power over Achilles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Solon
snapshots.body: The Athenian lawgiver, quoted in Book 1 on the limitlessness of wealth, and credited in Book 2 with laws against unlimited land ownership and with reshaping the Athenian constitution by opening the law courts to all citizens.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Midas
snapshots.body: The legendary king whose golden touch is cited as an example of wealth that cannot feed a man.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theodectes
snapshots.body: The tragedian whose play Helen is quoted for a line about noble birth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Daedalus
snapshots.body: The legendary craftsman, whose self-moving statues are cited as an image of tools needing no servants to operate them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hephaestus
snapshots.body: The god of craftsmanship, whose self-moving tripods are cited alongside the statues of Daedalus as an image of tools needing no servants.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amasis
snapshots.body: The Egyptian king, whose saying about his footpan is cited as an example of ceremony distinguishing a ruler from his subjects.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gorgias
snapshots.body: The rhetorician, cited in Book 1 for enumerating the virtues, and again in Book 3 (as "Gorgias of Leontini") for his ironic remark that citizens, like kettles, are manufactured by magistrates.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chares of Paros
snapshots.body: One of the writers on tillage and planting Aristotle cites. A different, unrelated "Chares" -- a political intermediary, not this agricultural writer -- appears later, in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apollodorus of Lemnos
snapshots.body: One of the writers on tillage and planting Aristotle cites, alongside Chares of Paros.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thales
snapshots.body: The philosopher, cited for his olive-press monopoly, told as an anecdote about how philosophers could be rich if they chose. Book 2 also reports (and calls chronologically inconsistent) a tradition making a "Thales" the teacher of Lycurgus and Zaleucus -- most likely the same figure invoked by a strained legendary genealogy rather than a second, unnamed person.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleisthenes of Athens
snapshots.body: The Athenian reformer who, after the expulsion of the tyrants, enrolled strangers, slaves, and resident aliens into new tribes (3:5) and later strengthened the democracy by similar measures (6:11). A different, unrelated Cleisthenes -- his maternal grandfather, the tyrant of Sicyon -- appears in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pheidon the Corinthian
snapshots.body: An ancient legislator credited with the view that the number of citizen families should remain fixed. A different, unrelated Pheidon -- a king of Argos who became a tyrant -- appears in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippodamus
snapshots.body: The son of Euryphon, of Miletus: inventor of the grid-plan city and layout of the Piraeus, and the first non-statesman to write on the ideal constitution -- his own three-class model occupies most of Book 2's discussion of him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lycurgus
snapshots.body: The traditional lawgiver of Sparta, credited with its constitution and common meals, said to have studied the Cretan constitution during King Charilaus's minority.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charilaus
snapshots.body: The Spartan king whose minority Lycurgus is said to have guarded before traveling to Crete (2:53). A later reference to "the tyranny of Charilaus at Lacedaemon" (5:78) is puzzling, since nothing elsewhere calls this legitimate king a tyrant; it is bound here as the same figure for lack of any textual signal of a second Charilaus, but the description does not obviously fit him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Minos
snapshots.body: The legendary king of Crete, credited with the laws still followed by its subject population and with Crete's naval empire; said to have died in Sicily. Cited again in Book 7 alongside Sesostris as an ancient founder of a warrior-versus-husbandmen class system.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ephialtes
snapshots.body: The Athenian statesman who, with Pericles, curtailed the power of the Areopagus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pericles
snapshots.body: The Athenian statesman who, with Ephialtes, curtailed the power of the Areopagus and instituted payment for jury service.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zaleucus
snapshots.body: The lawgiver who gave laws to the Epizephyrian Locrians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Onomacritus
snapshots.body: A Locrian by birth trained in Crete, sometimes credited (on chronologically dubious authority) as the first legislator with any special skill, and placed by that same tradition as Thales's teacher.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philolaus the Corinthian
snapshots.body: A Theban legislator of the Corinthian Bacchiad family, who left Corinth for Thebes out of horror at his mother Halcyone's incestuous passion for him, and there gave the Thebans their "Laws of Adoption."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diocles
snapshots.body: The Olympic victor and lover of Philolaus, who left Corinth with him over the same scandal that drove Philolaus away. Original-en prints the OCR-mangled "Diodes"; both spellings are aliased and the error is left as printed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Halcyone
snapshots.body: Diocles's mother, whose incestuous passion for her son drove him and Philolaus from Corinth to Thebes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Draco
snapshots.body: The Athenian lawgiver, noted only for the severity of his penalties.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pittacus
snapshots.body: Elected leader (an aesymnetia, or elective tyranny) by the Mitylenaeans against exiles led by Antimenides and the poet Alcaeus; also cited as a lawgiver for a law doubling penalties for drunken violence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antimenides
snapshots.body: One of the leaders of the exiles the Mitylenaeans elected Pittacus to oppose, named alongside the poet Alcaeus, his brother.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcaeus
snapshots.body: The poet, one of the leaders of the exiles opposed to Pittacus, quoted denouncing his own city for making the low-born Pittacus tyrant.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Androdamas of Rhegium
snapshots.body: Gave laws to the Chalcidians of Thrace, chiefly concerning homicide and heiresses.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phaleas of Chalcedon
snapshots.body: The first to propose that citizens of a state should have equal possessions; his equalization scheme and its limits occupy a long stretch of Book 2.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eubulus
snapshots.body: Talked Autophradates out of besieging Atarneus by pointing out the cost of the siege against the price of simply leaving.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Autophradates
snapshots.body: The besieger of Atarneus whom Eubulus talked out of the siege.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diophantus
snapshots.body: Introduced the plan at Athens under which artisans engaged on public works are treated as public slaves.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jason
snapshots.body: Quoted for the remark that he "felt hungry when he was not a tyrant" -- unable to bear living as a private citizen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euripides
snapshots.body: The tragedian, quoted on the special education of princes (Book 3), on living "according to one's fancy" as democratic license (Book 5), and elsewhere cited among those who scourged Decamnichus at Archelaus's court (Book 5).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lycophron
snapshots.body: The sophist, quoted for defining law as merely "a surety to one another of justice," a merely conventional guarantee rather than a maker of good citizens.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Achilles
snapshots.body: The Homeric hero, cited complaining of Agamemnon's treating him "like some dishonoured stranger."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agamemnon
snapshots.body: The Homeric king, cited both for dishonouring Achilles and, elsewhere, for his prayer wishing for ten wise counsellors.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antisthenes
snapshots.body: The Cynic philosopher, whose fable of the lions and the hares -- "where are your claws?" -- is cited against demands for equality from the unequal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heracles
snapshots.body: The legendary hero, said in myth to have been left behind by the Argonauts for fear he would overpower the rest of the crew -- an image for ostracism.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Periander of Corinth
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Corinth, son of Cypselus, named in full at 5:67 as "the great master" of the arts of tyranny; identifiable elsewhere by the corn-field anecdote he shares with Thrasybulus of Miletus (3:54, 5:52) and by the Cypselid dynasty's reign lengths (5:75, 5:76, forty-four years, ending in 5:76's note that he was "a great soldier"). A different, unrelated Periander -- the tyrant of Ambracia -- is named in full elsewhere in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thrasybulus of Miletus
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Miletus who received, via a herald, Periander of Corinth's wordless advice to cut down the tallest ears of corn -- meaning the leading citizens. A different, unrelated Thrasybulus -- Hiero's brother and successor as tyrant of Syracuse -- appears later in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysius I
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Syracuse, cited repeatedly across Books 1, 3, and 5: asking the Syracusans for a bodyguard as his first step to power (3:70), rising by denouncing the rich (5:19), installed by Hipparinus (5:21), the Locrian marriage connection blamed for ruining that city (5:29), grouped among demagogues-turned-tyrant (5:49), and taxing his subjects into poverty within five years (5:67). His son and successor, Dionysius II, is a different, explicitly "younger" Dionysius named later in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phocylides
snapshots.body: The gnomic poet, quoted praying for a middling competence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Telecles the Milesian
snapshots.body: Cited for a constitution in which citizens deliberate by turns rather than as a single body.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lysander
snapshots.body: The Spartan, said to have attempted to overthrow the Spartan monarchy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pausanias (Spartan king)
snapshots.body: A king of Sparta who attempted to overthrow the ephoralty (5:2) and whom the Lacedaemonians later accused of trying to seize personal power in the state (7:57, both places naming him explicitly as "king"). Two different, unrelated men also named Pausanias appear elsewhere in Book 5: the regent who commanded at Plataea, and Philip of Macedon's assassin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gelo
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Syracuse whose rise followed a period of democratic disorder there; his and his brother Hiero's dynasty is cited as the longest-lasting Syracusan tyranny, and its fall into a tyranny "distributed" among the family is discussed alongside Dionysius II's fall.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleomenes
snapshots.body: The Lacedaemonian king whose defeat of the Argives in the "Battle of the Seventh Day" forced Argos to admit some of its subject population to citizenship.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heracleodorus
snapshots.body: His accession to office at Oreum overthrew the oligarchy there and changed it into a constitutional, democratic government.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Paches
snapshots.body: The Athenian who took Mitylene in the war that followed a dispute there about heiresses.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Timophanes (Mitylene)
snapshots.body: A wealthy citizen of Mitylene whose two daughters, sought by Doxander for his own sons and refused, occasioned a revolution. A different, unrelated Timophanes -- the Corinthian general who seized a tyranny -- appears later in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Doxander
snapshots.body: Wanted Timophanes's daughters for his sons; rejected, he stirred up revolution and, as Athenian proxenus, drew in Athenian interference at Mitylene.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mnaseas
snapshots.body: The father of Mnason, on one side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mnason
snapshots.body: The son of Mnaseas, on one side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euthycrates
snapshots.body: The father of Onomarchus, on the other side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Onomarchus
snapshots.body: The son of Euthycrates, on the other side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phoxus
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Chalcis, killed by the people acting together with the notables, who then seized the government for themselves.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Peisistratus
snapshots.body: The Athenian tyrant, who rose by leading a faction against the men of the plain; his rule and his sons' (the Peisistratidae) is cited repeatedly as an example of both tyranny's origins and its fall, and, in one anecdote, of a tyrant submitting to trial before the Areopagus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Peisistratidae
snapshots.body: Peisistratus's family and dynasty at Athens, whose downfall -- provoked by the insult to Harmodius's sister -- and whose building projects (the temple of Olympian Zeus) are both cited.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theagenes
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Megara, who won popular favour by slaughtering the cattle of the wealthy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Daphnaeus
snapshots.body: One of the rich men whose denunciation by Dionysius I won him the people's confidence on his way to tyranny.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lygdamis
snapshots.body: A member of the oligarchy at Naxos who championed the oppressed people and afterward became tyrant himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Basilidae
snapshots.body: The family that ruled Erythrae well but was eventually deposed for the narrowness of its oligarchy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charicles
snapshots.body: Led the dominant faction among the Thirty at Athens, an example of a demagogue operating within a small oligarchy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phrynichus
snapshots.body: Led the dominant faction among the Four Hundred at Athens, an example of a demagogue operating within a small oligarchy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Simos
snapshots.body: Held the government at Larissa along with the Aleuadae family.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Aleuadae
snapshots.body: The ruling family of Larissa, who held the government there alongside Simos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Iphiades
snapshots.body: Associated with the political clubs that held power at Abydos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleotimus
snapshots.body: Introduced Chalcidian colonists at Amphipolis and then stirred them up against the rich.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hipparinus
snapshots.body: Installed Dionysius I as tyrant at Syracuse.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chares
snapshots.body: A political intermediary whose negotiation at Aegina became the occasion for an attempt to revolutionize the state there -- almost certainly the well-known Athenian general and mercenary commander, though the text gives no epithet to confirm it. A different, unrelated "Chares of Paros," an agricultural writer, is named in full in Book 1.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Timophanes (Corinth)
snapshots.body: The Corinthian general who, given command of mercenaries, made himself tyrant -- the brother the celebrated liberator Timoleon later killed for it, though Aristotle does not name Timoleon here. A different, unrelated Timophanes -- an ordinary wealthy citizen of Mitylene -- appears earlier in Book 5.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diagoras
snapshots.body: Overturned the oligarchy of the knights at Eretria after being wronged in a marriage dispute.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eurytion
snapshots.body: Punished at Heraclea on a charge of adultery in a judgment executed in a spirit of party rather than justice, provoking revolution.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archias
snapshots.body: Punished at Thebes on a charge of adultery in a judgment executed in a spirit of party rather than justice, provoking revolution.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Partheniae
snapshots.body: The illegitimate sons of the Spartan peers, who attempted a revolution at Sparta and, once detected, were sent away to colonize Tarentum.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cinadon
snapshots.body: A brave man excluded from Sparta's honours, who conspired against the Spartans under Agesilaus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agesilaus
snapshots.body: The Spartan king under whom Cinadon conspired against the Spartans.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tyrtaeus
snapshots.body: The poet whose "Good Order" is cited as evidence that citizens ruined by the Messenian War wanted a redistribution of land.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pausanias (the regent)
snapshots.body: Named as "general in the Persian War," cited as an example of an individual great enough to want to rule alone. Two different, unrelated men also named Pausanias appear elsewhere in Book 5: a Spartan king, and Philip of Macedon's assassin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hanno
snapshots.body: A Carthaginian, cited alongside Pausanias as an example of an individual great enough to want to rule alone.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Codrus
snapshots.body: Cited as a king who prevented his state from being enslaved in war, an example of royalty earned by benefiting one's people.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cyrus
snapshots.body: Cyrus the Great, cited as a king who gave his country freedom (5:50), and again as an example of a general who successfully attacked a monarch he despised -- his grandfather Astyages, whose power he judged worn out by soft living (5:59).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pheidon
snapshots.body: A king of Argos who became a tyrant, cited among rulers who extended hereditary power into outright tyranny. A different, unrelated Pheidon -- an ancient legislator -- is named in full ("Pheidon the Corinthian") in Book 2.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phalaris
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Acragas, cited as an example of a tyrant who rose from holding a great office rather than from being a demagogue.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Panaetius
snapshots.body: Rose from demagogue to tyrant at Leontini; later cited again as an example of an oligarchy that changed directly into a tyranny.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cypselus
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Corinth and father of Periander, who rose as a demagogue, ruled without ever needing a bodyguard, and founded the Cypselid dynasty (thirty years' reign, then Periander's forty-four); his family's costly public offerings are cited as a device for keeping subjects poor and occupied.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Harmodius
snapshots.body: The public dishonour of his sister, and the insult to himself, provoked the attack on the Peisistratidae that he and Aristogeiton carried out.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristogeiton
snapshots.body: Joined Harmodius in the attack on the Peisistratidae, for Harmodius's sake.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Periander of Ambracia
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Ambracia, expelled by the people acting with conspirators (5:15) and named in full ("Periander, the tyrant of Ambracia") as the target of a conspiracy provoked by an obscene question he asked a favourite youth (5:54). A different, unrelated Periander -- the tyrant of Corinth -- is Book 5's other, far more frequently cited Periander.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philip
snapshots.body: Philip II of Macedon, attacked by his own guard Pausanias after being permitted to suffer an insult from Attalus and his friends.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pausanias (assassin of Philip)
snapshots.body: Attacked Philip of Macedon after being permitted to suffer an insult from Attalus and his friends -- the historical assassin of Philip II, identified here by the surrounding narrative rather than an epithet. Two different, unrelated men also named Pausanias appear elsewhere in Book 5: a Spartan king, and the regent who commanded at Plataea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Attalus
snapshots.body: Insulted Pausanias, with the friends who joined him, provoking the attack on Philip of Macedon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyntas the Little
snapshots.body: Attacked by Derdas after boasting of having enjoyed Derdas's youth. A different, unrelated Amyntas -- Archelaus's own son -- is named later in the same passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Derdas
snapshots.body: Attacked Amyntas the Little after being boasted of.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Evagoras
snapshots.body: The king of Cyprus, slain by a eunuch avenging the eunuch's wife, whom Evagoras's own son had carried off.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Crataeus
snapshots.body: Attacked and killed Archelaus, ostensibly over a broken marriage promise involving Archelaus's daughters, though Aristotle judges the real cause was Crataeus's disgust at their intimate connection.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archelaus
snapshots.body: The Macedonian king killed by Crataeus; the subject of several further conspiracies recounted in Book 5 (Hellanocrates, Decamnichus) arising from broken promises and personal insults.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sirrhas
snapshots.body: The enemy Archelaus was fighting when he married his elder daughter to the king of Elymaea for military support.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arrhibaeus
snapshots.body: Named alongside Sirrhas as an enemy Archelaus was fighting when he married his elder daughter to the king of Elymaea for military support.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyntas (son of Archelaus)
snapshots.body: Archelaus's own son, married to Archelaus's younger daughter in hope of avoiding a quarrel with the son of Cleopatra. A different, unrelated Amyntas the Little is named earlier in the same passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleopatra
snapshots.body: A Macedonian royal woman, mother of the son Archelaus hoped to keep from quarrelling with his own son Amyntas -- not the later, far better-known queen of Egypt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hellanocrates of Larissa
snapshots.body: Archelaus's lover, who conspired against him after Archelaus failed to keep his promise of restoring him to his own country.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Parrhon
snapshots.body: Killed Cotys with Heracleides of Aenos to avenge their father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heracleides of Aenos
snapshots.body: Killed Cotys with Parrhon to avenge their father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cotys
snapshots.body: The Thracian king killed by Parrhon and Heracleides of Aenos in revenge for their father, and mutilated Adamas as a child, provoking Adamas's own later revolt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adamas
snapshots.body: Revolted from Cotys in revenge for being mutilated by him as a child.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megacles
snapshots.body: Attacked and killed the Penthalidae at Mitylene with his friends, after they had gone about the city assaulting people with clubs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Penthalidae
snapshots.body: A ruling clan at Mitylene, killed by Megacles and his friends after going about assaulting people with clubs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Smerdis
snapshots.body: Beaten and torn from his wife by Penthilus, whom he later killed in revenge.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Penthilus
snapshots.body: Beat Smerdis and tore him from his wife, and was later killed by him in revenge.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Decamnichus
snapshots.body: Led the assassins in the conspiracy against Archelaus, enraged after Archelaus handed him over to Euripides to be scourged for a remark about the poet's bad breath.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artapanes
snapshots.body: Conspired against and killed Xerxes, fearing he would be blamed for hanging Darius without orders.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Xerxes
snapshots.body: The Persian king, killed by Artapanes; also cited among rulers whose empires the Persian king (an earlier, unnamed reference) crushed rebellious former subjects.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Darius
snapshots.body: Hanged, apparently on Artapanes's own initiative rather than Xerxes's orders -- probably Xerxes's own son of this name, distinct from Darius I "the Great."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sardanapalus
snapshots.body: The legendary Assyrian king, slain by a courtier who saw him carding wool among his women -- an example of contempt as a motive for conspiracy. Named only in modern-en; original-en's text is corrupted at this point and never supplies the name (see the package README).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dion
snapshots.body: Attacked and expelled his own relative Dionysius II out of contempt for his drunkenness, landing with only a small force on the principle that even a quick death would be an honourable risk.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysius II
snapshots.body: Dionysius I's son and successor as tyrant of Syracuse, explicitly called "the younger Dionysius," attacked out of contempt and then expelled by his own relative Dion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Astyages
snapshots.body: Cyrus's grandfather and the Median king Cyrus overthrew, his power judged worn out by an effeminate life.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Seuthes
snapshots.body: A Thracian who conspired against Amadocus, the ruler whose general he was.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amadocus
snapshots.body: The Thracian ruler against whom his own general Seuthes conspired.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mithridates
snapshots.body: Conspired against Ariobarzanes out of a mix of contempt and love of gain.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariobarzanes
snapshots.body: The ruler against whom his own subordinate Mithridates conspired.

snapshots.name: Theopompus
snapshots.body: The Spartan king who further limited royal power (chiefly by establishing the Ephoralty), reasoning that a reduced but more durable kingship was a better inheritance for his sons than a greater but less secure one.

snapshots.name: Hiero
snapshots.body: Gelo's brother and successor as tyrant of Syracuse, whose spies and informers are cited as a model of tyrannical surveillance; succeeded in turn by his own brother Thrasybulus.

snapshots.name: Thrasybulus (Syracuse)
snapshots.body: Hiero's brother, who flattered Gelo's son into excess in order to rule through him, provoking the family conspiracy that ended the dynasty (5:63); he later succeeded Hiero as tyrant in his own right, only to be driven out within eleven months (5:76). A different, unrelated Thrasybulus of Miletus is Book 5's other, far more frequently cited Thrasybulus.

snapshots.name: Myron

snapshots.name: Cleisthenes of Sicyon
snapshots.body: The Orthagorid tyrant of Sicyon, respected for his military ability and said to have crowned the judge who ruled against him in the games. His rule followed Myron's (5:78) within the century-long Orthagorid tyranny (5:74). A different, unrelated Cleisthenes -- his own grandson, the Athenian democratic reformer -- appears in Books 3 and 6.
